The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference

Hiari Pizzini Cavagna hiari.pizzinicavagna@unibo.it    Andrea Proia    Daniele Cesarini    Zeynep Kiziltan    Andrea Bartolini organization=DEI - University of Bologna, city=Bologna, country=Italy organization=DISI - University of Bologna, city=Bologna, country=Italy organization=CINECA, city=Casalecchio di Reno, country=Italy
Abstract

Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and no law names the factors that set it. The most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. What is therefore needed is a law expressed in the architecture’s own hyperparameters, one that names which of them govern the cost of a token, explicitly accounts for attention mechanism, and applies to unseen LLMs. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity. From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families (OPT, LLaMA, Gemma, Falcon, Qwen2, and Granite) on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2=0.969R^{2}=0.969 and 11.97%11.97\% MAPE, 3.1−3.5×3.1-3.5\times below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3×3\times relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14×3.14\times across a 4.0×4.0\times reasoning-budget range. Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0×13.0\times relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and the KV-cache terms with input length; while prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (−93%-93\%), the KV-cache term is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8×4.8\times more. An interactive implementation of SIMPLE is available at ecs-lab/SIMPLE.

1 Introduction

Inference, not training, is where most of the energy of a Large Language Model (LLM) is spent: a model is trained once and then served continuously, and inference accounts for up to 90% of its life-cycle energy [15]. Yet for an LLM not yet deployed, the only dependable way to know that cost is to build it, serve it, and measure it, an answer that arrives once the architecture is no longer a choice. The target is also moving: reasoning spends additional tokens to buy accuracy [21], while agentic workflows [7] have pushed median prompt lengths from 750–1050 to 68K tokens [18].

The token is the unit of account of this economy. Inference is priced, billed, budgeted, and benchmarked per token [35], and capacity is planned in tokens per second and tokens per joule. Yet no analytical model states what a token costs, and no law names the factors that set it. A token is an observable of the workload, not a unit of computational work: each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so average token energy depends on input length, generation length, context reuse, and how attention is organized. The consequence is already visible in the economics: using a model with a lower listed price per token can incur up to 28×28\times the total cost of using a nominally more expensive one [4]. An entire industry settles in a currency whose production cost cannot be computed.

Energy models exhibit the same gap in analytical form. Prior work fits energy as a function of input and output lengths [38, 43, 40, 24] empirically, without deriving it from the computational kernels, thereby describing a measured regime rather than explaining it. SweetSpot [26], the most accurate analytical formulation reported to date, removes the decisive obstacle by deriving the decode phase in closed form from the computation and memory accesses of decoder-only Transformer inference. SweetSpot, however, is a fit, not a law. Its coefficients are identified on a single LLM and carry that LLM’s architecture implicitly: the number of layers, the hidden dimension, and the organization of attention never appear as terms. The formulation therefore neither names the factors that set the cost of a token nor applies to a model it has not already measured, and later analytical models [36, 11, 22] relax this only in part.

This limitation is felt where decisions are now being made: in energy efficiency. Intelligence per Watt relates delivered capability to the power that produced it [27], and serving is reported in tokens per joule [35], but both are measured on systems that already exist. They rank deployments after the fact and cannot say which architecture would deliver the same capability for less, how many reasoning tokens are worth spending [21], or at what context length serving an agentic request ceases to be affordable [18]. A measured efficiency locates no optimum. What is therefore needed is a law expressed in the architecture’s own hyperparameters, one that explains which of them govern the energy of a token, predicts that energy for an LLM never benchmarked, and thereby turns efficiency from something observed into something derived.

Modern LLMs share the decoder-only Transformer [37] and differ in a handful of hyperparameters and attention architectures: Multi-Head Attention (MHA) has largely given way to Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) [1] and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) [9], each cutting memory traffic and KV-cache size, and with them the energy per generated token [26]. Furthermore, long generations, 68K-token contexts, and mandatory prefix caching push today’s requests precisely into the regime where the KV-cache term dominates: no law of token cost can be blind to how attention is organized.

Together, these considerations motivate the following open research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: Is there an analytical model that can accurately predict inference energy across LLMs with different architectures, including the attention mechanism?

  • •

    RQ2: Can an LLM-agnostic model remain compact and accurate enough to be a practical alternative to LLM-specific models, while generalizing to unseen LLM architectures and workloads?

  • •

    RQ3: How do LLM size and architectural hyperparameters influence inference energy consumption?

  • •

    RQ4: How does the reasoning token budget affect inference energy and Intelligence per Joule?

  • •

    RQ5: How does the energy cost of a single query shift from non-agentic to agentic workloads?

This work answers these with the following contributions:

  • •

    We present a taxonomy of state-of-the-art LLM inference energy models, classified by functional form, grounding theory, and ability to predict inference energy across LLMs with different architectures, including the attention mechanism. We find that the most accurate model, SweetSpot [26], absorbs architectural information implicitly into its fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM calibration and making it neither LLM-agnostic nor attention-aware. The SOTA therefore lacks an analytical model capable of accurately predicting the energy consumed by a generic request for an arbitrary LLM.

  • •

    To close this gap, we analytically derive closed-form expressions for the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference, covering both MHA and GQA mechanisms Building on these, we propose the SIMPLE law, which separately models prefill and decode energy costs, further decomposing the latter into the self-attention KV-cache cost and the next-token computation (i.e., the feed-forward network). Validated against a family of analytically derived models spanning different fitting granularities and modeling approaches, SIMPLE achieves the best accuracy-compactness trade-off among the evaluated models, reducing the error of SOTA models by 3.13.1–3.5×3.5\times.

  • •

    Applying the SIMPLE law across LLMs of different sizes, families, and architectures, we show that hidden dimension dd is the most sensitive architectural hyperparameter, as prefill energy scales quadratically with dd, while layer depth contributes linearly. Attention architecture matters strongly: more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces per-token energy by up to 3×3\times relative to standard MHA, making it an impactful architectural choice for reducing inference energy.

  • •

    We use the SIMPLE law to analytically derive the output length τo​u​t\tau_{out} that minimizes per-token energy (the sweet spot), showing that increasing the reasoning token budget pushes τo​u​t\tau_{out} beyond this minimum, driving super-linear energy growth. Although accuracy grows with the reasoning budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence Per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14×3.14\times at the lowest and highest budgets across a 4.0×4.0\times range.

  • •

    Using the SIMPLE law, we analyze the energy cost of agentic AI workloads and show that energy per request increases by 13.0×13.0\times relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and KV-cache terms with input length. While prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%93\%), the KV-cache term, accounting for 86%86\% of the remaining energy, is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request still costs 4.8×4.8\times more than a non-agentic one.

We evaluate our models on a large dataset [26] of TensorRT-LLM [23] traces collected from a set of widely used dense LLMs running on NVIDIA H100. The included models span model sizes and architectures, covering OPT [44], LLaMA [14], Gemma [33], Falcon [2], Qwen2 [41], and Granite [20].

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. After providing background in Section 2, we review related work in Section 3. Then we derive the floating point and memory operations of LLM inference in Section 4, and building on this, we present in Section 5 SIMPLE, together with the family of complexity-derived models used throughout the evaluation. In Section 6 we experimentally validate SIMPLE, and discuss in Section 7 how model size, architectural hyperparameters, reasoning, and agentic workloads impact energy consumption. Finally, we conclude in Section 8.

2 Background

This section introduces the background needed for the analysis in this work. We briefly review the fundamentals of LLM architectures, their computational characteristics, and the metrics used throughout the paper.

LLM Architecture

LLMs are built on the Transformer architecture [37], which has become the standard for generative AI. A Transformer block consists of two main components, the Multi-Head Self-Attention Mechanism (MHA) and the Feed-Forward Network (FFN), each wrapped in residual connections, layer normalization, and dropout. In MHA, the hidden representation is projected into several subspaces, corresponding to different heads. Each head learns to capture a different type of dependency within the sequence, and the head outputs are then combined. This improves the model’s expressivity and its ability to represent diverse relationships, but it also increases the number of operations in proportion to the number of heads. To reduce this overhead, Multi-Query Attention (MQA) was proposed in 2019 [29]. It keeps multiple query heads but shares a single set of Key-Value (KV) projections across all of them, which drastically reduces memory usage and KV-cache size during decoding and makes inference more efficient. More recently, Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) was introduced in 2023 [1] as a generalization of MHA and MQA: keys and values are shared within groups of heads, striking a balance between the efficiency of MQA and the expressivity of MHA. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced with DeepSeek-V2 [9], provides a different mechanism to reduce the KV-cache footprint. Rather than sharing KV projections across heads, it compresses keys and values into a single low-rank latent vector. The full per-head keys and values are then recovered from this latent through up-projection matrices, preserving the expressivity of MHA at a fraction of the memory cost. Despite its distinct compression mechanism, MLA can nonetheless be seen as a variant of GQA [5].

LLM Inference Computation

In large-scale models, most of the learnable weights, referred to as parameters, reside in the FFN layers, whereas the runtime complexity is dominated by the attention mechanism, owing to its quadratic dependence on the input sequence length. The total number of parameters, typically in the billions, is referred to as model size. LLM inference is typically split into two phases: prefill, in which the entire input sequence is processed in parallel to initialize the KV-cache, and decode, in which tokens are generated autoregressively [42]. During prefill, the computational cost is dominated by the quadratic attention term; during decode, thanks to the reuse of cached keys and values, the cost per token grows only linearly with the sequence length. Nevertheless, for long outputs, the decode phase often accounts for most of the total inference time, since tokens must be produced one at a time, which restricts the opportunities for parallelization. On modern GPUs, the throughput of LLM inference is constrained not only by arithmetic performance but also by memory bandwidth. Storing and retrieving the large KV-cache during decoding places considerable stress on the memory subsystem. For example, in autoregressive decoding, every generated token requires loading all previous keys and values from memory, which makes attention kernels strongly memory-bound, especially for long contexts.

Metrics and Measurement

We define the total energy consumption Etot​(τin,τout)E_{\text{tot}}(\tau_{\text{in}},\tau_{\text{out}}), expressed in Joules, as the energy the GPU consumes to process a given request, characterized by an input length τin\tau_{\text{in}} and an output length τout\tau_{\text{out}}. Normalizing EtotE_{\text{tot}} by τout\tau_{\text{out}} yields the Energy-per-Token EtokE_{\text{tok}}:

Etok=Etotτout​[JoulesToken]E_{\text{tok}}=\frac{E_{\text{tot}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}\hskip 9.24994pt\left[\frac{\mathrm{\text{Joules}}}{\mathrm{\text{Token}}}\right]

We also define energy efficiency EeffE_{\text{eff}} as the reciprocal of EtokE_{\text{tok}}, capturing the number of output tokens generated per unit of energy. Finally, to relate energy consumption to the quality of the generated output, we adopt the Intelligence per Joule (IPJ) metric [27]. We compute it as the ratio of task accuracy to the energy required to process a request:

IPJ=AccEtot​[Accuracy %Joule]\text{IPJ}=\frac{\text{Acc}}{E_{\text{tot}}}\hskip 9.24994pt\left[\frac{\mathrm{\text{Accuracy $\%$}}}{\mathrm{\text{Joule}}}\right]

where Acc is the accuracy averaged over the evaluated queries and EtotE_{\text{tot}} is the average per-request energy, making it a practical metric for realistic deployment scenarios.

3 Related Work

Recent work on LLM inference energy falls broadly into two categories: (i) experimental characterization of energy consumption, and (ii) analytical or empirical models for predicting it. We review each in turn, then position our contributions with respect to the identified limitations.

3.1 Experimental Characterizations

Several studies have characterized LLM inference energy across different workloads and hardware conditions. Samsi et al. [28] benchmark energy for LLaMA models of varying sizes across two NVIDIA GPU generations (V100 and A100), including multi-node and multi-GPU execution. Chung et al. [6] introduce ML.ENERGY, a benchmark suite for measuring energy under realistic serving conditions across different tasks, and show that automated configuration recommendations can reduce consumption. Stojkovic et al. [31] study how inference server configurations affect latency, throughput, and energy. Maliakel et al. [19] examine the effect of GPU Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) settings on energy for different workloads. Fernandez et al. [13] analyze energy across inference optimization strategies and task types. Wilhelm et al. [39] investigate the accuracy–energy trade-off, focusing on how inference strategies such as chain-of-thought affect it.

Unlike the following works, none of these proposes an energy prediction model.

3.2 Predictive Models

Recent studies have proposed models to predict the energy consumption of LLM inference. These models focus on the number of input and output tokens (τin\tau_{\text{in}} and τout\tau_{\text{out}}), while not explicitly accounting for batch size. Batch size is instead commonly incorporated into models targeting distributed inference [17, 25], whereas it is generally not considered in models for single-GPU inference, as in our setting.

The following paragraphs review the state-of-the-art models, grouped by EtotE_{\text{tot}} functional form and further characterized by three criteria that directly reflect the limitations our work addresses. First, whether they are analytically derived from first principles, such as Transformer computational complexity, or are empirical. Second, whether they must be fitted separately for each LLM. We refer to models that require a per-LLM fit as LLM-specific, and to those that do not as LLM-agnostic. Third, whether they are attention-aware, meaning that they explicitly account for different attention mechanisms, rather than assuming standard MHA. Table 1 summarizes all reviewed models along these criteria.

Linear Models

A common empirical approach is to assign a fixed cost to input and output sequence lengths, yielding a linear model:

Etot≈θ0+θ1​τin+θ2​τoutE_{\text{tot}}\approx\theta_{0}+\theta_{1}\tau_{\text{in}}+\theta_{2}\tau_{\text{out}}

Both Vellaisamy et al. [38] and Zhan et al. [43] propose linear models, though they differ in how they handle input-length dependence. Vellaisamy et al. focuses solely on decode energy absorbing the prefill cost into a fixed constant, effectively modeling decode energy as linear in τout\tau_{\text{out}} alone, while Zhan et al. make τin\tau_{\text{in}} an explicit term as in the formulation above. Neither model is derived from first principles or includes architectural hyperparameters, so both must be fitted separately for each LLM and are not attention-aware.

Zhan et al. [43] apply their model to Vision-Language Models and additionally propose an LLM-agnostic formulation that scales with model size SS (in billions of parameters):

Etot≈θ0+θ1​S+θ2​τin+θ3​τout+θ4​S​τin+θ5​S​τoutE_{\text{tot}}\approx\theta_{0}+\theta_{1}S+\theta_{2}\tau_{\text{in}}+\theta_{3}\tau_{\text{out}}+\theta_{4}S\tau_{\text{in}}+\theta_{5}S\tau_{\text{out}}

While this formulation is LLM-agnostic, model size serves as the only architectural proxy, capturing scale but not structural hyperparameters such as the number of layers, hidden dimension, or attention configuration.

Bilinear Models

Wilkins et al. [40] and Delavande et al. [11] extend the linear formulation with an interaction term between input and output sequence lengths:

Etot≈θ0+θ1​τin+θ2​τout+θ3​τin​τoutE_{\text{tot}}\approx\theta_{0}+\theta_{1}\,\tau_{\text{in}}+\theta_{2}\,\tau_{\text{out}}+\theta_{3}\,\tau_{\text{in}}\tau_{\text{out}}

Wilkins et al. motivate the interaction term statistically, using ANOVA to confirm that input and output lengths have a significant joint effect on energy, and fit the model empirically via ordinary least squares. Delavande et al. derive the same form analytically from the roofline model: the interaction term reflects the cumulative cost of attending to a growing context at each decode step. Neither model includes architectural hyperparameters, thus both must be fitted separately for each LLM and are not attention-aware.

Power-law Models

Oviedo et al. [24] propose a bottom-up framework that estimates per-query inference energy from node power draw and token throughput:

Etot=PUE3.6⋅Pnode⋅LeffTPS​(τin,τout)E_{\text{tot}}=\frac{\text{PUE}}{3.6}\cdot\frac{P_{\text{node}}\cdot L_{\text{eff}}}{\text{TPS}(\tau_{\text{in}},\,\tau_{\text{out}})}

where PUE accounts for data-center overhead, PnodeP_{\text{node}} is the measured steady-state node power, TPS​(τin,τout)\text{TPS}(\tau_{\text{in}},\tau_{\text{out}}) is fitted empirically to per-model benchmarks as a piecewise log-linear regression, and Leff≈τoutL_{\text{eff}}\approx\tau_{\text{out}} scales energy by output length. Because TPS is linear in log⁡τin\log\tau_{\text{in}} and log⁡τout\log\tau_{\text{out}}, substituting it into the formula yields a power-law dependence on sequence lengths:

Etot≈θ0​τinθ1​τoutθ2E_{\text{tot}}\approx\theta_{0}\,\tau_{\text{in}}^{\theta_{1}}\,\tau_{\text{out}}^{\theta_{2}}

The framework includes no architectural hyperparameters; thus the throughput model must be re-fitted for each LLM, making the approach LLM-specific and not attention-aware.

Quadratic Models

SweetSpot [26] models inference energy as proportional to FLOPs and data transfers, analytically derived from the transformer computational kernels as a function of τin\tau_{\text{in}} and τout\tau_{\text{out}}. The decoding phase is handled by expressing the growing KV-cache context as an arithmetic series, which yields a closed-form quadratic formulation:

Etot≈θ0+θ1​τin+θ2​τin2+θ3​τin​τout+θ4​τout+θ5​τout2E_{\text{tot}}\approx\theta_{0}+\theta_{1}\,\tau_{\text{in}}+\theta_{2}\,\tau_{\text{in}}^{2}+\theta_{3}\,\tau_{\text{in}}\tau_{\text{out}}+\theta_{4}\,\tau_{\text{out}}+\theta_{5}\,\tau_{\text{out}}^{2}

The model reduces the MAPE of the bilinear baseline from over 30%30\% to below 2%2\%. However, the fitted coefficients are LLM-specific, requiring an exhaustive measurement dataset for each target model. The approach therefore cannot generalize to unseen architectures or be applied during training. Moreover, the analytical derivation treats all QQ, KK, and VV projection matrices as having the same hidden dimension dd, implicitly assuming standard MHA. Since the attention mechanism is not parameterized in the formulation, SweetSpot is not attention-aware.

Following a similar analytical approach, Vartziotis et al. [36] decompose inference energy into compute and memory-access components:

Etot≈αTC​CTC+eHBM​B​η​(N)E_{\text{tot}}\approx\alpha_{\text{TC}}\,C_{\text{TC}}+e_{\text{HBM}}\,B\,\eta(N)

where CTCC_{\text{TC}} denotes the total tensor-core FLOP count for prefill and decode, and BB denotes the total HBM traffic. CTCC_{\text{TC}} and BB are derived analytically from the transformer computational graph, following a similar decomposition to [26], though the FLOP count CTCC_{\text{TC}} relies on the Kaplan training parameter-scaling approximation [16] (C≈K​N​TC\approx KNT, K=6K=6 FLOPs per parameter per token) rather than an inference kernel-by-kernel tally. The factor η⁡(N)\eta(N), where NN is the number of model hyperparameters, is a dimensionless inefficiency multiplier that accounts for non-ideal HBM bandwidth utilization, while αTC\alpha_{\text{TC}} and eHBMe_{\text{HBM}} are hardware-specific energy coefficients for tensor-core and HBM operations, expressed in pJ/FLOP and pJ/bit respectively (H100 GPU, FP16/BF16). Because αTC\alpha_{\text{TC}} and eHBMe_{\text{HBM}} are hardware constants rather than fitted per-model coefficients, and CTCC_{\text{TC}} and BB are expressed in terms of NN and structural hyperparameters such as layer count and hidden dimension, the model is LLM-agnostic and captures the order-of-magnitude energy and scaling trends observed in authors’ measurements.

However, its accuracy is limited, with a reported mean relative error of approximately 20%20\%. Furthermore, expanding CTCC_{\text{TC}} and BB yields a long closed-form expression in the architectural hyperparameters, which makes the model hard to interpret and limits its usefulness for identifying the hyperparameters that drive energy consumption. Similarly to SweetSpot, the model assumes MHA, so the reduced KV-cache traffic of GQA, which is standard in many modern LLMs, is not captured by the model.

To the best of our knowledge, Niu et al. [22] is the only existing work to propose an attention-aware energy model for LLM inference. Their model estimates the energy per output token of a single decode step, expressing decode energy as a linear function of the bytes accessed, considering both the model weights and the KV-cache, and the measured decode time. The KV-cache byte term is analytically derived from the model architecture and attention mechanism: it is explicitly parametrized by the number of KV heads per layer (Nk​vN_{kv}), which accounts for MHA and GQA. The decode time, however, must be measured at runtime. The resulting model requires a separate calibration and fit for each LLM and hardware configuration. Since the model covers only the decode phase energy, excluding the prefill, it is not directly applicable to predict the total inference energy EtotE_{\text{tot}} for a given query, which is the focus of this work. We therefore do not consider it further here.

3.3 SIMPLE Model

The box above summarizes the answer to RQ1. We address the key limitations of previous approaches by extending the derivation of the computational and memory-access complexities of SweetSpot [26] to GQA, and using the resulting expressions to derive SIMPLE, a compact LLM-agnostic model that explicitly represents the attention mechanism, builds on SweetSpot’s interpretable quadratic structure to expose the role of individual architectural hyperparameters, and predicts energy across multiple LLM architectures without per-LLM calibration.

Throughout our study, we target the Energy-per-Token EtokE_{\text{tok}}, rather than total energy consumption EtotE_{\text{tot}}, since normalizing by τout\tau_{\text{out}} isolates the cost of generation from the cost of processing the input, exposing the trade-off between amortizing the prefill cost over more output tokens and incurring additional decode cost as τout\tau_{\text{out}} grows. Moreover, EtokE_{\text{tok}} serves as a natural unit for comparison across different workloads and deployments, as it corresponds directly to operational metrics such as cost-per-token and tokens-per-joule, matching how inference is commonly priced and provisioned in production.

4 FLOPs and MemOPs Formulation

In this section, we present the analytical derivation of the Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs) and Memory Operations (MemOPs) of LLM inference based on a decoder-only Transformer, distinguishing the prefill and decode phases and assuming no quantization of weights or KV-cache. In the following derivations, we consider a dense LLM and a constant batch size, extending the derivation of SweetSpot [26] to include the GQA mechanism.

For a matrix multiplication between 𝐀∈ℝm×k\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k} and 𝐁∈ℝk×n\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}, we denote the number of FLOPs and MemOPs as FF and MM respectively, calculated as:

F\displaystyle F =2​m​n​k\displaystyle=2mnk
M\displaystyle M =mk+kn+mn(read 𝐀, read 𝐁, write result)\displaystyle=mk+kn+mn\quad\text{(read }\mathbf{A}\text{, read }\mathbf{B}\text{, write result)}

We neglect bias additions, layer normalization, softmax, and dropout, as their cost is negligible relative to projections and FFN layers. Moreover, we treat the FFN expansion factor as a fixed constant (4×\times), consistent with the original decoder-only Transformer design and still the dominant convention across dense LLM architectures, even though some models in our evaluation set adopt slightly different ratios.

Table 2 describes the symbols we use throughout the paper. In order to model both MHA and GQA, we define the KV-to-query head ratio RR as the ratio between the number of KV heads nkvn_{\text{kv}} and the number of query heads nqn_{\text{q}}. We consider the KV projections as weight matrices of shape d×d⋅R=d×dkvd\times d\cdot R=d\times d_{\text{kv}}, reflecting that in GQA only nkv≤nqn_{\text{kv}}\leq n_{\text{q}} key and value heads are materialized. For MHA, nkv=nqn_{\text{kv}}=n_{\text{q}} and all expressions reduce to the standard form.

4.1 Prefill FLOPs and MemOPs

During prefill, the full input sequence of length τin\tau_{\text{in}} is processed in parallel.

Attention Projections

QPQ_{P} projection XP​WQX_{P}W_{Q}:

FQP=2​τin​d2MQP=τin​d+d2+τin​d=2​τin​d+d2\displaystyle\hskip 15.00002pt\begin{aligned} F_{Q_{P}}&=2\,\tau_{\text{in}}\,d^{2}\\ M_{Q_{P}}&=\tau_{\text{in}}d+d^{2}+\tau_{\text{in}}d=2\tau_{\text{in}}d+d^{2}\end{aligned} (1)

KP,VPK_{P},V_{P} projections XP​WKX_{P}W_{K} and XP​WVX_{P}W_{V}:

FKP=FVP=2​τin​d2​RMKP=FVP=τin​d+d2​R+τin​d​R\displaystyle\hskip 15.00002pt\begin{aligned} F_{K_{P}}=F_{V_{P}}&=2\,\tau_{\text{in}}\,d^{2}\,R\\ M_{K_{P}}=F_{V_{P}}&=\tau_{\text{in}}d+d^{2}R+\tau_{\text{in}}dR\end{aligned} (2)

FYP=2×2​τin​d⋅4​d=16​τin​d2MYP=τin​d+4​d2+4​τin​d+4​τin​d+4​d2+τin​d=10​τin​d+8​d2\displaystyle\hskip 15.00002pt\begin{aligned} F_{Y_{P}}&=2\times 2\,\tau_{\text{in}}\,d\cdot 4d=16\,\tau_{\text{in}}\,d^{2}\\ M_{Y_{P}}&=\tau_{\text{in}}d+4d^{2}+4\tau_{\text{in}}d+4\tau_{\text{in}}d+4d^{2}+\tau_{\text{in}}d\\ &=10\,\tau_{\text{in}}d+8\,d^{2}\end{aligned} (6)

With LL layers, the total prefill FLOPs is:

Fprefill=L⁡[FPproj+FSP+FAP+FYP]=L⁡[4​τin​d2​(5+R)+4​τin2​d]\displaystyle\hskip 13.28143pt\begin{aligned} F_{\mathrm{prefill}}&=L\!\left[F_{P_{\mathrm{proj}}}+F_{S_{P}}+F_{A_{P}}+F_{Y_{P}}\right]\\ &=L\!\left[4\,\tau_{\text{in}}\,d^{2}\!\left(5+R\right)+4\tau_{\text{in}}^{2}d\right]\end{aligned} (7)

At each decode step t∈[1,…,τout]t\in[1,\ldots,\tau_{\text{out}}], one new token is generated autoregressively. The KV-cache at step tt holds (τin+t−1\tau_{\text{in}}+t-1) tokens: the τin\tau_{\text{in}} input tokens and t−1t-1 previously generated tokens.

FSD​(t)=2​(τin+t−1)​dMSD​(t)=d+(τin+t−1)​d​R+(τin+t−1)​nq\displaystyle\hskip 11.99998pt\begin{aligned} F_{S_{D}}(t)&=2(\tau_{\text{in}}+t-1)d\\ M_{S_{D}}(t)&=d+(\tau_{\text{in}}+t-1)\,dR+(\tau_{\text{in}}+t-1)\,n_{\text{q}}\end{aligned} (12)

FAD​(t)=2​(τin+t−1)​dMAD​(t)=(τin+t−1)​nq+(τin+t−1)​d​R+d\displaystyle\hskip 11.99998pt\begin{aligned} F_{A_{D}}(t)&=2(\tau_{\text{in}}+t-1)d\\ M_{A_{D}}(t)&=(\tau_{\text{in}}+t-1)\,n_{\text{q}}+(\tau_{\text{in}}+t-1)\,dR+d\end{aligned} (13)

FYD​(t)=16​d2MYD​(t)=d+4​d2+4​d+4​d+4​d2+d=10​d+8​d2\displaystyle\hskip 11.99998pt\begin{aligned} F_{Y_{D}}(t)&=16d^{2}\\ M_{Y_{D}}(t)&=d+4d^{2}+4d+4d+4d^{2}+d\\ &=10\,d+8\,d^{2}\end{aligned} (14)

Total OPs

Using the closed-form sum:

∑t=1τoutt=τout​(τout+1)2\displaystyle\hskip 15.00002pt\begin{aligned} \sum^{\tau_{\text{out}}}_{t=1}t=\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}(\tau_{\text{out}}+1)}{2}\end{aligned}

and summing over τout\tau_{\text{out}} generated tokens and LL layers, we obtain the total decode FLOP count:

Fdecode=L​∑t=1τout[FDproj+FSD​(t)+FAD​(t)+FYD​(t)]=L​∑t=1τout[4​d2​(5+R)+4​d​(τin+t−1)]=L⁡[4​d2​τout​(5+R)+4​d​(τout​τin+τout​(τout−1)2)]\displaystyle\hskip 8.8543pt\begin{aligned} F_{\mathrm{decode}}&=L\sum^{\tau_{\text{out}}}_{t=1}\!\left[F_{D_{\mathrm{proj}}}+F_{S_{D}}(t)+F_{A_{D}}(t)+F_{Y_{D}}(t)\right]\\ &=L\sum^{\tau_{\text{out}}}_{t=1}\!\left[4d^{2}\!\left(5+R\right)+4d(\tau_{\text{in}}+t-1)\right]\\ &=L\left[4d^{2}\tau_{\text{out}}\left(5+R\right)+4d\left(\tau_{\text{out}}\tau_{\text{in}}+\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}(\tau_{\text{out}}-1)}{2}\right)\right]\end{aligned} (15)

5 SIMPLE Derivation

In this section, we present the formulation of SIMPLE, the proposed analytical model for predicting the energy efficiency of LLM inference, for a generic LLM architecture f⁡(d,L,nq,nkv)f(d,L,n_{\text{q}},n_{\text{kv}}) and the input/output sequence f⁡(τin,τout)f(\tau_{\text{in}},\tau_{\text{out}}). The model is built on the complexity analysis introduced in the previous section, more precisely on Equations (1–14). These equations offer different valid groupings of their inner terms according to the number of fitting coefficients, each implying a different interpretation for each coefficient.

A first approach we propose is to assign a meaning to each coefficient in terms of Joule/FLOPs or Joule/MemOPs. We refer to these models as OPs-centric. A second orthogonal approach is to drop the interpretation but preserve only the relational one with respect to f⁡(τin,τout)f(\tau_{\text{in}},\tau_{\text{out}}). We refer to these models as IO-centric. In these formulations, we include the LLM architectural hyperparameters (d,L,nq,nkvd,L,n_{\text{q}},n_{\text{kv}}) in order to obtain LLM-agnostic models. While the OPs-centric models serve as an exploratory baseline, SIMPLE is ultimately derived within the IO-centric family.

The proposed models are summarized in Table 3. As direct comparisons, we include the EtokE_{\text{tok}} formulations of SweetSpot [26] and the two LLM-agnostic models from related work: Vartziotis et al. [36], which can be classified as OPs-centric as it explicitly assigns meaning to its terms, and Zhan et al. [43], which falls among the IO-centric models.

5.1 OPs-centric Approach

We formulate three models that assign a meaning to each coefficient in terms of Joule/FLOPs and Joule/MemOPs at different levels of granularity.

FLOPs-MemOPs

The first formulation assigns one coefficient to Equations (7, 15) and another to Equations (8, 16):

Etok=θ0+θ1​Fprefill+Fdecodeτout+θ2​Mprefill+MdecodeτoutE_{\text{tok}}=\theta_{0}+\theta_{1}\frac{F_{\text{prefill}}+F_{\text{decode}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}+\theta_{2}\frac{M_{\text{prefill}}+M_{\text{decode}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}} (17)

The model assumes that these two components contribute independently to the total inference energy, assigning a separate cost to each, regardless of whether the operations are performed in the prefill or the decode phase.

Prefill-Decode

The second formulation differentiate these energy costs by prefill and decode phases, and assigns individual coefficients to Equations (7, 15, 8, 16), allowing the model to capture potentially different operating conditions and energy costs of the two phases:

Etok=θ0+θ1​Fprefillτout+θ2​Fdecodeτout+θ3​Mprefillτout+θ4​MdecodeτoutE_{\text{tok}}=\theta_{0}+\theta_{1}\frac{F_{\text{prefill}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}+\theta_{2}\frac{F_{\text{decode}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}+\theta_{3}\frac{M_{\text{prefill}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}+\theta_{4}\frac{M_{\text{decode}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}} (18)

Fine-Grained

The third formulation maximizes the fitting granularity assigning a coefficient to each intermediate term, but perishing the physical meaning of Joule/FLOPs and Joule/MemOPs:

Etok=θ0+∑i=124θi​L​Ciτout,E_{\text{tok}}=\theta_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{24}\theta_{i}\,\frac{L\,C_{i}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}, (19)

where:

Ci∈{FQP,MQP,…​∑t=1τoutFAD​(t),∑t=1τoutMAD​(t)}C_{i}\in\left\{F_{Q_{P}},M_{Q_{P}},\ldots\sum_{t=1}^{\tau_{\text{out}}}{F_{A_{D}}(t)},\sum_{t=1}^{\tau_{\text{out}}}{M_{A_{D}}(t)}\right\}

denotes the complexity of each intermediate term across prefill and decode from Equations (1–6, 9–14).

5.2 IO-centric Approach

The previous models explore different ways of incorporating the analytical FLOPs and MemOPs into the energy prediction model. While these formulations explicitly account for the underlying computational cost, they also introduce a growing number of terms and fitting coefficients. The IO-centric approach instead groups the complexity terms according to their dependency on f⁡(τin,τout)f(\tau_{\text{in}},\tau_{\text{out}}), simplifying or discarding those of negligible contribution.

In the following paragraphs, we first introduce LLM-agnostic SweetSpot, a natural extension of SweetSpot, [26] used as a comparison baseline, then present SIMPLE.

LLM-agnostic SweetSpot

The SweetSpot model [26] captures quadratic dependencies on f⁡(τin,τout)f(\tau_{\text{in}},\tau_{\text{out}}), but is fitted for individual LLMs. All architectural information is implicitly absorbed into the learned coefficients, making it impossible to generalize across different LLM architectures. A natural extension is therefore to preserve SweetSpot’s functional dependencies on f⁡(τin,τout)f(\tau_{\text{in}},\tau_{\text{out}}) while making the coefficients explicitly dependent on the LLM architecture f⁡(d,L,nq,nkv)f(d,L,n_{\text{q}},n_{\text{kv}}). To this end, we group the complexity terms from Equations (7, 8, 15, 16) to match the corresponding terms of the SweetSpot formulation reported in Table 3.

Etok=\displaystyle E_{\text{tok}}= θ0+θ1​τin2τout​L​(4​d+2​nq)+θ2​τin​L​(4​d+2​d​R+2​nq)\displaystyle\theta_{0}+\theta_{1}\,\frac{\tau_{\text{in}}^{2}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}\,L\left(4d+2n_{\text{q}}\right)+\theta_{2}\,\tau_{\text{in}}\,L\left(4d+2dR+2n_{\text{q}}\right) (20)
+\displaystyle+ θ3​τinτout​L​[d2​(4​R+20)+d⁡(4​R+18)]\displaystyle\theta_{3}\,\frac{\tau_{\text{in}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}\,L\left[d^{2}\left(4R+20\right)+d\left(4R+18\right)\right]
+\displaystyle+ θ4​τout​L​(2​d+d​R+nq)+θ5τout​L​d2​(2​R+10)\displaystyle\theta_{4}\,\tau_{\text{out}}\,L\left(2d+dR+n_{\text{q}}\right)+\frac{\theta_{5}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}\,L\,d^{2}\left(2R+10\right)
+\displaystyle+ θ6​L​[d2​(6​R+30)+d⁡(2​R+18)−2​d−(d​R+nq)]\displaystyle\theta_{6}L\left[d^{2}\left(6R+30\right)+d\left(2R+18\right)-2d-\left(dR+n_{\text{q}}\right)\right]

The resulting formulation preserves the SweetSpot dependencies while explicitly incorporating the architectural complexity of the target LLM, thereby enabling generalization across multiple LLM architectures. However, despite sharing a similar number of fitting coefficients and functional dependencies with SweetSpot, this formulation involves a considerable number of terms, similarly to the previously derived Fine-Grained model, since it groups complexity terms without assessing their individual significance or exploring optimal grouping strategies. As a consequence, it provides limited insights into how each architectural parameter and inference phase contributes to energy consumption.

SIMPLE

To obtain a compact, interpretable, and generalizable model, we systematically evaluated different simplification and term-aggregation strategies, starting from Equations (7, 8, 15, 16). In particular, we adopted three complementary methods to refine the model. First, we performed term ablations, removing inner terms with low statistical significance. Second, we simplified the resulting expressions by discarding lower-order terms. Third, we explored different grouping strategies for the remaining terms. Based on these refinement methods, we derived the following EtotE_{\text{tot}} formulation of SIMPLE:

Etot=θ1​d2​L​τin⏟Prefill+OPENθ2​d​L​R​(τin​τout+τout22CLOSE⏞KV-cache)+(θ0+θ3​d​L)​τout⏞Next-token⏟DecodeE_{\text{tot}}=\underbrace{\theta_{1}\,d^{2}L\,\tau_{\text{in}}\vphantom{\Big(\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}^{2}}{2}\Big)}}_{\text{\small Prefill}}+\underbrace{\overbrace{\theta_{2}d\,L\,R\Big(\tau_{\text{in}}\tau_{\text{out}}+\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}^{2}}{2}\vphantom{\Big(\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}^{2}}{2}\Big)}}^{\text{\small KV-cache}}\Big)+\overbrace{(\theta_{0}+\theta_{3}d\,L\,)\tau_{\text{out}}\vphantom{\Big(\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}^{2}}{2}\Big)}}^{\text{\small Next-token}}\vphantom{\Big(\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}^{2}}{2}\Big)}}_{\text{\small Decode}}

where the total energy consumption combines the cost of the Prefill and Decode phases.

The Prefill term accounts for processing the input prompt and is obtained by refining Equations (7,  8). It scales linearly with the input length τin\tau_{\text{in}} and the number of layers LL, and quadratically with the hidden dimension dd. The Decode component covers the generation of the output tokens and is obtained by refining Equations (15, 16). It comprises two terms. The KV-cache term captures the cost of reading the KV-cache, which grows as the context lengthens with each generated token. The Next-token term represents the cost that accumulates at a constant rate per generated token. Both terms scale linearly with dd and LL, while the KV-cache term additionally scales with the KV-to-query head ratio RR.

The fitting coefficients θi\theta_{i} weigh each term independently, assigning a distinct cost to each phase and separating the KV-cache cost from the Next-token cost. Dividing by the number of generated tokens τout\tau_{\text{out}} yields the per-token formulation EtokE_{\text{tok}} of SIMPLE:

Etok=θ1​d2​L​τinτout⏟Prefill Amortization+θ2​d​L​R​(τin+τout2)⏞KV-cache+θ0+θ3​d​L⏞Next-token⏟Decode AccumulationE_{\text{tok}}=\underbrace{\fcolorbox{prefillcol}{white}{$\displaystyle\vphantom{\left(\tau_{\text{in}}+\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}}{2}\right)}\theta_{1}\, d^2 L\, \frac{\tau_{\text{in}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}$}}_{\mathclap{\text{\small Prefill Amortization}}}+\underbrace{\overbrace{\fcolorbox{kvcol}{white}{$\displaystyle\vphantom{\left(\tau_{\text{in}}+\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}}{2}\right)}\theta_{2}\, d\, L\, R \left( \tau_{\text{in}} + \frac{\tau_{\text{out}}}{2} \right)$}}^{\mathclap{\text{\small KV-cache}}}+\overbrace{\fcolorbox{nexttokcol}{white}{$\displaystyle\vphantom{\left(\tau_{\text{in}}+\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}}{2}\right)}\theta_{0} + \theta_{3}\, d\, L$}}^{\mathclap{\text{\small Next-token}}}}_{\mathclap{\text{\small Decode Accumulation}}} (21)

The Prefill term becomes a Prefill Amortization term, reflecting how the fixed cost of processing the prompt is spread over the generated tokens. The Decode term becomes a Decode Accumulation term, in which the KV-cache cost grows linearly with the context length, and the Next-token cost reduces to a constant per generated token.

6 Experimental Validation

This section details the experimental study conducted to validate SIMPLE. Section 6.1 describes the dataset 11 1 Publicly available on Zenodo: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18714476 introduced in [26] and reused in our experiments, summarizing its key observations on energy consumption, namely the relevance of the attention mechanism and the non-linear relationship with input and output lengths. Section 6.2 presents our results 22 2 The evaluation code is available at gitlab.com/ecs-lab/simple-law.

6.1 Dataset Description

The dataset contains energy measurements of TensorRT-LLM inference traces collected from a diverse set of widely used dense LLMs running on NVIDIA H100 accelerators. The included models span a range of LLM sizes and architectures, including MHA and on GQA with different KV grouping ratios, using a standard bf16 format for weights and KV-cache. The full list of models is given in Table 4.

The dataset comprises synthetic requests processed using trtllm-bench configured in throughput mode, with request concurrency set to 1000 and a maximum batch size of 1024. The maximum sequence length and the maximum number of batched tokens are both set to 8192. The experiments were conducted using one GPU per run on a server equipped with an Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ CPU and four NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPUs connected via NVLink. Input and output lengths independently span 64–4096 tokens in powers of two, yielding 49 combinations with 1000 requests each. GPU power was sampled every 500 ms using pynvml [8]. The per-query energy was obtained by multiplying the average GPU power over 1000-request by the total measurement time, and dividing by the number of requests. Since neither the baseline models nor the SIMPLE model explicitly accounts for batching, we use these fixed settings, and fit energy per individual request.

Figure 1 reports the average tokens per joule computed on the 49 different workload configurations across the different LLMs in the dataset. Smaller models and GQA-based architectures generally achieved higher efficiency (Figure 1): Llama 3.2 1B reached 55.91 tok/J, compared with 5.12 tok/J for Falcon-RW 7B. Among similarly sized models, Qwen2 1.5B (GQA R=1/7) achieved 49.06 tok/J versus 20.66 tok/J for OPT 1.3B (MHA R=1). This underlines the importance of modeling the attention architecture alongside other LLM architectural hyperparameters. Model size alone is not enough to characterize inference energy consumption.

Figure 2 reports an aggregated average of the tokens per joule computed on the different models across the 49 different workload configurations in the dataset. Efficiency generally peaked at short inputs (τin=64\tau_{\text{in}}=64) and intermediate outputs (τout∈[128,256]\tau_{\text{out}}\in[128,256]), and was lowest for long inputs and short outputs. Across models, the best configuration was (33.41±4.90)×(33.41\pm 4.90)\times more efficient than the worst. These results showed a model-dependent energy-efficiency “sweet spot” associated with model size, attention architecture, and sequence lengths. These findings provide the basis for the extended analysis presented here.

6.2 Experimental Results

In this section, we evaluate the accuracy of the proposed SIMPLE model in predicting the energy per token against that of the SOTA models and the other OPs-centric and IO-centric models reported in Table 3. All models have been fitted using Weighted Least Squares (WLS), since the variance of the measured token energy increases with the number of processed tokens, indicating heteroscedasticity.

Table 5 reports the results of this comparison across three evaluation protocols: (i) Leave-One-Out Cross Validation (LOOCV), which evaluates generalization to previously unseen LLM architectures by withholding the corresponding architectural hyperparameters (dd, LL, nqn_{\text{q}}, nkvn_{\text{kv}}) during fitting; (ii) kk-fold cross validation, which evaluates model stability and robustness using 10-fold cross validation with 5 repetitions over individual (tin,tout)(t_{\mathrm{in}},t_{\mathrm{out}}) observations randomly shuffled across the complete dataset, ensuring each fold contains samples from all 13 architectures, in both the training and test sets, and (iii) full-dataset fit, used to generate the final fitting coefficients for energy estimation. In the table, columns correspond to the fitted models and rows report the accuracy results under each protocol. Figure 3 shows the values reported in Table 5, except for SweetSpot, whose scale would otherwise compress the remaining variants, at the expense of readability. We then use the full-dataset fit coefficients to compare SIMPLE against LLM-specific models on the same dataset. For each model and validation protocol, we report the coefficient of determination (R2R^{2}) and the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). All three protocols show similar comparative results.

Cross Validation

When comparing LOOCV results, SOTA approaches of Zhan et al. [43] and Vartziotis et al. [36] achieve R2R^{2} values of 0.4560.456 and 0.6450.645, respectively. The proposed LLM-agnostic SweetSpot outperforms SOTA models, reaching an R2R^{2} of 0.7800.780, showing that extending the previously proposed SweetSpot formulation with LLM architectural hyperparameters makes it LLM-agnostic, able to predict across LLMs without separate per-model fits, improving MAPE from 69.444 to 30.390. Despite being more accurate than SOTA models, its accuracy is far from optimal. Among OPs-centric models, Fine-Grained is the most accurate, reaching R2=0.945R^{2}=0.945, while FLOPs-MemOPs and Prefill-Decode obtain substantially lower R2R^{2} of 0.5510.551 and 0.5220.522, respectively. This shows that considering only one coefficient per operation (FLOPs and MemOPs) or per inference phase lowers the attainable accuracy, which drops by 2.7×2.7\times in MAPE compared to Fine-Grained.

The proposed SIMPLE model, which groups fine-grained terms into an interpretable formulation consisting of the terms corresponding to Prefill, KV-cache and Next-token costs, reduces the fitting coefficients by 6.25×6.25\times and achieves the highest accuracy, with an R2R^{2} of 0.9440.944 and a MAPE of 13.252%13.252\%, compared to 0.9450.945 and 14.208%14.208\% for the Fine-Grained model, while compared to the SOTA models, SIMPLE achieves a MAPE of 2.82.8–3.4×3.4\times lower.

The kk-fold results confirm the trends observed with LOOCV, with only minor differences due to the different nature of the validation task. Together, these results show that SIMPLE generalizes well to unseen LLM architectures (LOOCV) and interpolates effectively, accurately predicting unseen workload configurations of known LLMs (kk-fold).

Finally, on the full dataset, SIMPLE reaches an R2R^{2} of 0.9690.969 and a MAPE of 11.97411.974, confirming the small accuracy gap with Fine-Grained observed under cross validation. The resulting coefficients are used throughout the paper and are reported in Table 9 in Appendix A.

To validate our OPs-centric approach, which aims to give a physical meaning to the fitted coefficients, we also report the coefficients of the OPs-centric FLOPs-MemOPs model. The estimated energy per FLOP (1.86×10−121.86\times 10^{-12} J) and per memory operation (4.317×10−124.317\times 10^{-12} J) are on the order of picoJoules, consistent with the measured energy per operation of Tensor Cores and HBM in NVIDIA GPUs [3].

Comparison with LLM-specific Models

Table 6 compares the full-dataset fit of SIMPLE with SOTA LLM-specific models [38, 43, 11, 40, 24, 26], which are fitted separately for each LLM; for these we report the mean and standard deviation of R2R^{2} and MAPE across LLMs in the dataset. The previously proposed SweetSpot [26] model achieves the highest accuracy among SOTA formulations, with a near-perfect in-sample fit (mean R2=1.000R^{2}=1.000, mean MAPE =1.841%=1.841\%). This sets an upper bound on the accuracy attainable by the proposed LLM-agnostic model. The architecture-aware terms of SIMPLE allow it to remain LLM-agnostic: a single set of coefficients covers all architectures, with no per-model fitting. This generality comes at a cost in accuracy, with MAPE increasing from 1.841% to 11.974%, while R2R^{2} decreases only slightly, from 1.000 to 0.969.

Nevertheless, SIMPLE outperforms all other LLM-specific baselines in both R2R^{2} and MAPE. Its MAPE is 41.5% lower than that of the bilinear models [11, 40], and 3.2×\times and 5.3×\times lower than those of the linear [38, 43] and power-law [24] models, resp. The box above summarizes the answer to RQ2.

7 Use Cases of the SIMPLE Law

The accuracy and generalizability of SIMPLE, demonstrated in Section 6, establish its analytical formulation beyond a predictive model: its architecture-aware terms allow it to be applied as a law, from which structural insights on LLM inference energy can be derived. In this section, we apply SIMPLE as such to explain a family of notable trade-offs in LLM inference: (i) how LLM size and architecture f⁡(d,L,R)f(d,L,R) impact EtokE_{\text{tok}} (Section 7.1), (ii) how input/output sequence f⁡(τin,τout)f(\tau_{\text{in}},\tau_{\text{out}}) yields an energy minimum in EtokE_{\text{tok}}, and how this minimum shapes EtotE_{\text{tot}}, and, through it, the Intelligence per Joule attained under increasing reasoning token budgets (Section 7.2), and (iii) how EtotE_{\text{tot}} of a single query shifts from non-agentic to agentic AI workloads (Section 7.3). We use the SIMPLE law coefficients fitted on the full dataset (coefficients θ\theta in Table 9).

To aid readability, we recall here the three contributions of the SIMPLE law to EtokE_{\text{tok}}, color-highlighted consistently with the figures:

θ1​d2​L​τinτout⏟Prefill Amortizationθ2​d​L​R​(τin+τout2)⏞KV-cacheθ0+θ3​d​L⏞Next-token⏟Decode Accumulation\underbrace{\fcolorbox{prefillcol}{white}{$\displaystyle\vphantom{\left(\tau_{\text{in}}+\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}}{2}\right)}\theta_{1}\, d^2 L\, \frac{\tau_{\text{in}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}}$}}_{\mathclap{\text{\small Prefill Amortization}}}\quad\underbrace{\overbrace{\fcolorbox{kvcol}{white}{$\displaystyle\vphantom{\left(\tau_{\text{in}}+\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}}{2}\right)}\theta_{2}\, d\, L\, R \left( \tau_{\text{in}} + \frac{\tau_{\text{out}}}{2} \right)$}}^{\mathclap{\text{\small KV-cache}}}\quad\overbrace{\fcolorbox{nexttokcol}{white}{$\displaystyle\vphantom{\left(\tau_{\text{in}}+\frac{\tau_{\text{out}}}{2}\right)}\theta_{0} + \theta_{3}\, d\, L$}}^{\mathclap{\text{\small Next-token}}}}_{\mathclap{\text{\small Decode Accumulation}}}

7.1 Impact of LLM Size and Architecture on Energy

Figure 4 shows the contribution of each SIMPLE law term to the predicted EtokE_{\text{tok}} as a function of the individual key architectural hyperparameters: the hidden dimension dd, the number of layers LL, and the KV-to-query head ratio R=nkv/nqR=n_{\text{kv}}/n_{\text{q}}. We set τin=τout=512\tau_{\text{in}}=\tau_{\text{out}}=512 and use Llama 3.1 8B architectural hyperparameters as a reference.

In Figure 4 (a), the Prefill Amortization term grows quadratically with dd, while the Decode Accumulation terms grow only linearly: the KV-cache term is proportional to dd, and the Next-token term is affine in dd due to the constant offset θ0\theta_{0}. This quadratic dependence dominates the overall scaling, producing a rapid increase in EtokE_{\text{tok}} for large hidden dimensions and marking dd as one of the most sensitive LLM architectural design hyperparameter. Moreover, it suggests that the energy penalty of LLMs with a larger dd is amplified in prefill-dominated scenarios where long contexts are paired with short outputs.

The number of layers LL, shown in Figure 4 (b), multiplies the Prefill Amortization and KV-cache terms, and the θ3​d​L\theta_{3}dL component of the Next-token term. Only the constant offset θ0\theta_{0} is independent of LL, so EtokE_{\text{tok}} grows proportionally with model depth. Finally, Figure 4 (c) shows the energy impact of the attention head configuration. The Decode Accumulation KV-cache is the only term that depends on RR. It scales linearly with τin\tau_{\text{in}} and τout\tau_{\text{out}}, so a smaller RR (i.e., a larger 1/R=nq/nkv1/R=n_{\text{q}}/n_{\text{kv}}, corresponding to more aggressive GQA grouping) reduces the KV-cache cost during decoding, making LLM architectures with higher GQA grouping more efficient on long output sequences. In the given example, EtokE_{\text{tok}} is ≈\approx60 mJ/tok under R=1/7R=1/7, compared to ≈\approx150 mJ/tok under standard MHA (R=1R=1), a reduction of approximately 3×3\times. How do these dependencies impact the token energy consumption across (i) LLMs of the same family with growing size and (ii) LLMs of the same size but different families?

Figure 5 shows the contribution of each SIMPLE term to the predicted EtokE_{\text{tok}} at τin=τout=512\tau_{\text{in}}=\tau_{\text{out}}=512, using Llama 3.2 1B as the reference and comparing it against three other models: Qwen2 1.5B and OPT 1.3B, which are similar in size, and Llama 3.1 8B, which belongs to the same family but is larger. Qwen2 1.5B shows an EtokE_{\text{tok}} similar to Llama 3.2 1B (15 vs. 14 mJ/tok) but a different breakdown: its smaller dd (1536 vs. 2048) and RR (1/6 vs. 1/4), partially offset by a larger LL (28 vs. 16), reduce the KV-cache share from 48% to 39%; the combined effect of its smaller dd and larger LL keeps the Prefill Amortization nearly unchanged, while increasing the Next-token share from 35% to 46%. At longer sequences, these structural differences favor Qwen2 1.5B, whose lower KV-cache coefficient increasingly dominates, making it more energy-efficient than Llama 3.2 1B. A starker contrast is seen with OPT 1.3B, which has the same dd as Llama 3.2 1B but a larger LL (24 vs. 16) and uses MHA (R=1R=1) instead of GQA (R=1/4R=1/4). As a result, the KV-cache share grows from 48% to 78%, increasing the KV-cache energy from 6 mJ/tok to 40 mJ/tok, resulting in an overall EtokE_{\text{tok}} increase from 14 mJ/tok to 51 mJ/tok. Comparing Llama 3.2 1B with the larger Llama 3.1 8B, the Prefill Amortization share increases from 17% to 26% while the KV-cache share decreases from 48% to 38%: as both dd (4096 vs. 2048) and LL (32 vs. 16) double, Prefill Amortization grows 8×8\times while the KV-cache term grows only 4×4\times, due to the quadratic contribution of dd, despite the same RR.

These results show that the SIMPLE law explains the energy differences between LLMs (Figure 1) as well as their expected scalability to longer input/output sequences through the architectural hyperparameters that drive each inference phase, which model size alone cannot capture. The box above summarizes the answer to RQ3.

7.2 From Energy Minimum to Reasoning Efficiency

Throughout, Qwen3-1.7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B to derive the EtokE_{\text{tok}} minimum analytically and to map EtokE_{\text{tok}} over a wide input/output token range and connect EtotE_{\text{tot}} to Intelligence per Joule.

EtokE_{\text{tok}} and Input/Output Sequence

Figure 7 shows the predicted EtokE_{\text{tok}} for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B as a function of τout\tau_{\text{out}}, with τin\tau_{\text{in}} fixed at an arbitrary length of 64. The colored regions correspond to the additive components of the SIMPLE law (Prefill Amortization, and Decode Accumulation, comprising separate KV-cache and Next-token regions), with the black curve giving the total. The Prefill Amortization energy cost decreases as 1/τout1/\tau_{\text{out}}, so its EtokE_{\text{tok}} decreases hyperbolically as more output tokens are generated. In contrast, the Decode Accumulation cost of the KV-cache term increases linearly with τout\tau_{\text{out}}, reflecting the accumulation of KV-cache entries with each new output token. The remaining cost of the Next-token term is independent of the output length and contributes a constant energy. The balance between the decreasing prefill contribution and the increasing decode contribution produces a minimum in the EtokE_{\text{tok}} curve, corresponding to the sweet spot [26] of inference energy efficiency. The location of this optimum can be obtained analytically from the SIMPLE law by differentiating EtokE_{\text{tok}} with respect to τout\tau_{\text{out}} and setting the derivative to zero. Since dd and LL are strictly positive by definition, the common factor d​L>0dL>0 can be divided out, yielding:

∂Etok∂τout=−θ1​d​τinτout2+θ2​R2=0\frac{\partial E_{\text{tok}}}{\partial\tau_{\text{out}}}=-\,\theta_{1}d\,\frac{\tau_{\text{in}}}{\tau_{\text{out}}^{2}}+\theta_{2}\,\frac{R}{2}=0

Solving for τout\tau_{\text{out}} yields the optimal output sequence length:

τout∗=2​θ1θ2​1R​d​τin=2​θ1θ2​nqnkv​d​τin\tau_{\text{out}}^{\ast}=\sqrt{2\,\frac{\theta_{1}}{\theta_{2}}\,\frac{1}{R}\,d\,\tau_{\text{in}}}=\sqrt{2\,\frac{\theta_{1}}{\theta_{2}}\,\frac{n_{\text{q}}}{n_{\text{kv}}}\,d\,\tau_{\text{in}}} (22)

This result gives a closed-form expression for the sweet spot, i.e., the output sequence length that minimizes the energy per generated token. In particular, the optimal output length grows proportionally to τin​d\sqrt{\tau_{\text{in}}d}, and is inversely proportional to the KV-to-query head ratio R=nkv/nq\sqrt{R}=\sqrt{n_{\text{kv}}/n_{\text{q}}}. Consequently, larger input lengths require longer generations to amortize the prefill cost, while architectures with a larger RR reach the energy optimum with shorter outputs.

Figure 6 shows the EtokE_{\text{tok}} landscape generated by the SIMPLE law, over the input token range [16,65536][16,65536] and output token range [4,16384][4,16384], using Qwen3-1.7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B architectural hyperparameters. These spans cover the LLM workloads used in conversation and coding [32], agentic [18] and reasoning [21, 30]. Both predicted landscapes closely mirror the non-linear efficiency pattern empirically observed in the dataset of [26] (Figure 2), capturing both the prefill-amortization and the decode-dominated regimes within a single surface. For a fixed τin\tau_{\text{in}}, the surface exhibits the expected amortization effect, with EtokE_{\text{tok}} reaching a minimum before rising again as the linear decode cost dominates. For the shortest input (τin=16\tau_{\text{in}}=16), this minimum lies at τout≈64\tau_{\text{out}}\approx 64 tokens for Qwen3-1.7B and τout≈128\tau_{\text{out}}\approx 128 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, and corresponds to the most energy-efficient point in the token space, at ≈\approx12 and ≈\approx30 mJ/tok, respectively. As τin\tau_{\text{in}} increases, the contours elongate along the output axis, reflecting the growing weight of the prefill term relative to the linear decoding contribution. The effect is strongest for short outputs, where the prefill cost is amortized over only a handful of tokens: the least energy-efficient point in the token space is located at τin=65​K\tau_{\text{in}}=65\text{K} and τout=4\tau_{\text{out}}=4, where EtokE_{\text{tok}} reaches ≈\approx66 J/tok for Qwen3-1.7B and ≈\approx293 J/tok for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B.

Reasoning Cost and Intelligence per Joule

Reasoning (or thinking) is widely referred to as the process of generating intermediate tokens before producing the final response, thereby leveraging additional test-time computation to improve accuracy [21, 30]. Throughout this section, we refer to the total number of generated tokens, including explicit reasoning tokens, as the reasoning token budget. Since SIMPLE already models all generated tokens as τout\tau_{\text{out}}, increasing the reasoning token budget directly increases τout\tau_{\text{out}} and hence EtotE_{\text{tot}}. To assess how this energy cost translates into reasoning efficiency, we combine the EtotE_{\text{tot}} predicted by SIMPLE with task accuracy, measured as Intelligence per Joule (IPJ == accuracy /Etot)/~E_{\text{tot}}). We draw on results from [30], which reported the accuracy of a set of SOTA LLMs (including Qwen3-1.7B [34] and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B [10]) on widely used benchmarks while varying reasoning budget.

From the results of [30], we report in Table 7 the accuracy as a function of the reasoning token budget for Qwen3-1.7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B on the AIME-24 dataset [45], for which both models report results across a comparable range of reasoning token budgets. In the same table, we also report the estimated EtokE_{\text{tok}} and EtotE_{\text{tot}} using the SIMPLE law, at the corresponding reasoning token budget, together with their ratios with respect to the minimum considered reasoning token budget, τout=2048\tau_{\text{out}}=2048. As input length, we use AIME-24 mean prompt length (τin=105\tau_{\text{in}}=105).

Figure 8 shows that accuracy increases consistently with the reasoning token budget τout\tau_{\text{out}} for both models, as does EtotE_{\text{tot}}. For Qwen3-1.7B, accuracy rises from 3.0% to 46.0% as τout\tau_{\text{out}} grows from 2048 up to 11896 tokens, corresponding to a reasoning budget 5.8×5.8\times the minimum. Over the same range, EtokE_{\text{tok}} rises from 43.6 mJ/tok up to 190.4 mJ/tok, increasing EtotE_{\text{tot}} by 25.4×25.4\times and lowering IPJ to 0.60×0.60\times of its initial value. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B shows a similar trend: accuracy improves from 2.0% to 44.0% as τout\tau_{\text{out}} grows from 2048 to 8145 tokens, increasing EtotE_{\text{tot}} by 10.4×10.4\times. Unlike Qwen3-1.7B, this causes an IPJ increase of 2.11×2.11\times.

Despite these opposite trends at the two reasoning extremes, both models show an IPJ peak neither at the minimum nor the maximum reasoning budget, but at an intermediate level, as visible in Figure 8(c). This arises because all reported budgets lie well past the EtokE_{\text{tok}} minimum predicted by SIMPLE (τout∗≈165\tau_{\text{out}}^{*}\approx 165 tokens for Qwen3-1.7B and ≈331\approx 331 tokens for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B), so EtotE_{\text{tot}} grows super-linearly as EtokE_{\text{tok}} and τout\tau_{\text{out}} increase together, while the marginal accuracy gain per additional token decreases. Concretely, at the IPJ peak, the accuracy gain exceeds the EtotE_{\text{tot}} increase for both models; for Qwen3-1.7B (4063 tokens), accuracy grows by 4.67×\times against EtotE_{\text{tot}} by 3.35×\times, yielding an IPJ gain of 1.39×\times; for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (3515 tokens), 7.5×\times against 2.38×\times, yielding an IPJ gain of 3.15×\times.

This application of the SIMPLE law provides a quantitative framework for identifying the reasoning budget that maximizes inference energy, measured as IPJ. The box above summarizes the answer to RQ4.

7.3 Energy Cost in Agentic Workloads

So far, SOTA works [11, 24, 12] have focused on evaluating the environmental impact of conversational AI. Agentic AI workloads are changing this landscape, and no existing work proposes a theoretical framework that can capture and explain the resulting transformation in energy cost, as they lack a way of accounting for prompt/prefix caching. Liu et al. [18] present an extensive analysis of the GitHub Copilot [7] coding agent production workload. Unlike conversational AI, characterized by queries with a median prompt length (τin\tau_{\text{in}}) of 750–1050 tokens and a median completion length (τout\tau_{\text{out}}) of 80–105, the reported agentic workload follows a long-tail distribution with a median context length (τin\tau_{\text{in}}) of 68K tokens and a median completion length of 247 tokens. Moreover, they report a median prefix KV-cache of 63K tokens, which corresponds to a hit rate of ≈93%\approx 93\%. This means that in the average query only 5K input tokens (out of 68K) are newly computed in the prefill stage.

We apply the SIMPLE law with the following adaptation. Let τc≤τin\tau_{\text{c}}\leq\tau_{\text{in}} be the number of input tokens served from the cache. Only the uncached suffix needs to be prefilled, so the Prefill Amortization term in the SIMPLE law ( θ1​d2​L​τin/τout\theta_{1}\,d^{2}L\,\tau_{\text{in}}/\tau_{\text{out}}) scales with τin−τc\tau_{\text{in}}-\tau_{\text{c}} instead of τin\tau_{\text{in}}.

Table 8 quantifies this effect for Llama 3.1 8B on the median GitHub Copilot request, comparing three scenarios. In the non-agentic scenario, for which we consider only the non-cached input (τin=5\tau_{\text{in}}=5K, τc=0\tau_{\text{c}}=0), the request costs 138.1 J, with Prefill (88.8 J) as the dominant term and the KV-cache contribution (43.2 J) playing a secondary role. Moving to the agentic scenario (τin=68\tau_{\text{in}}=68K, τc=0\tau_{\text{c}}=0), both context-dependent terms grow approximately proportionally to τin\tau_{\text{in}}: Prefill increases by 13.6×13.6\times and KV-cache by 13.3×13.3\times, while the Next-token term is unchanged, bringing EtotE_{\text{tot}} to 1787.7 J (13.0×13.0\times). Prefix caching (τin=68\tau_{\text{in}}=68K, τc=63\tau_{\text{c}}=63K) is highly effective on the Prefill term in this setting: only the 5K uncached tokens are processed, reducing Prefill contribution back to 88.8 J (−93%-93\%) and reducing EtotE_{\text{tot}} by 2.7×2.7\times (668.7 J). However, the agentic cached request still consumes 4.8×4.8\times more energy than the non-agentic one. This is because the KV-cache term is unaffected by prefix caching: the full 68K context must still be read and attended to at every decoding step, accounting for 86% of the remaining energy.

The last row reports the energy cost of generating one additional token (τout=248\tau_{\text{out}}=248). For the non-agentic request, it is 0.20 J. In the agentic scenario, it rises to 2.35 J (11.8×11.8\times), driven by KV-cache and Next-token energy growth, while the Prefill energy is unchanged. Since caching only affects Prefill, the cost of the additional generated token is identical in the agentic scenario with or without prefix caching. The box above summarizes the answer to RQ5.

8 Conclusions

This paper presented the SIMPLE law, an architecture-aware closed-form expression for predicting the energy cost of dense decoder-only LLM inference, derived from the computational and memory-access complexity of the prefill and decode phases. SIMPLE expresses energy consumption with a compact and interpretable formulation, which explains prefill and decode energy costs as a function of LLM architectural hyperparameters and input/output sequence lengths. By explicitly modeling the attention mechanism, SIMPLE closes a gap in the literature, as the first analytical energy law able to generalize across LLM architectures. With only four parameters fitted once across all LLMs, it reduces the error of previous SOTA models by 3.1–3.5×\times, reaching a MAPE of 11.97%.

Beyond predictive accuracy, the SIMPLE law quantitatively explains three of the most prominent effects in modern LLM inference: how LLM size and architecture affect energy cost, how the reasoning token budget drives super-linear energy growth and shapes the Intelligence per Joule, and how agentic AI transforms energy consumption. Taken together, these results establish the SIMPLE law as an analytical foundation for sustainable LLM inference.

Our approach is subject to a few limitations, which we group into three categories. First, our evaluation is restricted to dense, single-GPU LLMs and does not cover mixture-of-experts models. We also restrict our evaluation to MHA and GQA attention mechanisms; validation on more recent attention variants, LLM sizes, and architectures is left for future work. Second, the SIMPLE law does not explicitly model batch size or the number of concurrent requests as hyperparameters of the formulation. We plan to explicitly incorporate such additional workload parameters to extend the law. Finally, the reference dataset was collected using TensorRT-LLM on a single H100 GPU. Therefore, the SIMPLE law captures the energy behavior of single-device inference, and does not account for the additional costs of multi-GPU deployments, such as inter-device communication, tensor or pipeline parallelism, and distributed KV-cache management. As such, the fitted coefficients are specific to this hardware-framework pair. How the coefficients would change using other accelerators, multi-GPU deployments, and other inference frameworks remains to be explored in future work.
